lead: AR pays for itself where information belongs to a place or an object: a patient on the table, a page in a book, a machine on the line. The system tracks that place, draws a label or model over it, and shows the result on a display the worker or student already has. The same four questions apply everywhere: what is tracked, what is drawn, which display is used, and how the result was evaluated. This chapter walks through medicine, education, entertainment and industry with those questions fixed in view.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for the three AR requirements, 6.2 for display types, 6.3 for tracking families, 6.4 for toolkit calls, and 6.5 for interaction.

blocks.text: Surgical navigation is the clearest case. A pre-operative CT or MRI scan is segmented into tumour, vessels and bone. The system registers that scan to the patient on the table. Registration uses fiducial markers stuck on the skin, or a tracked surface probe, or a camera that matches the patient surface. The tracked object is the patient or a marker fixed to the patient; the camera pose is found every frame. The system draws the segmented structures and the planned cut plane over the real patient.

The display can be an optical see-through headset, a video see-through tablet, or a microscope with a combiner. The device is chosen for the task: a headset keeps the surgeon's hands free, a tablet is easier to share with a nurse. Evaluation uses target registration error in millimetres, task time and the number of corrective moves. A small error sounds good but may still be unsafe near a nerve.

Vein finding is projection AR. A near-infrared camera sees veins under the skin; a projector draws the vein map back onto the skin. Nothing is worn. Rehabilitation games track the hand or a marker and draw targets; the patient reaches for them. Anatomy teaching puts a marker on a plastic model and draws labels and cut-away views. Remote mentoring shares the operating field camera; an expert draws an arrow on the remote frame and the local surgeon sees it on a tablet.

items: What is tracked: patient marker, surface, or instrument.
What is drawn: tumour, vessels, cut plane, vein map, target.
Evaluation: registration error, time, safety, clinical score.

sections.h3: Education: page targets and safe practice

blocks.text: An AR book prints a page target. The phone camera finds the page, the app draws a 3D molecule or engine part standing on the page, and the student walks around it. The target is a printed image; the display is a phone or tablet. Chemistry and anatomy use the same pattern: a marker on a model, a label over the real object, a cut-away view that a flat diagram cannot show. Museums and historic sites use a marker, GPS or a visual map; the app draws a rebuilt wall or a person from the period over the ruin.

Laboratory and safety training uses AR to rehearse a procedure before touching the real equipment. A marker on a machine draws the next step, the correct valve, or the safe zone. The student can fail without damage. Evaluation is a checklist score, not a feeling of engagement.

Wireless displays appear in classroom AR: the teacher's tablet casts the camera view and the overlay to a projector. This removes the cable, but adds latency and battery load. The class sees the same target, yet the teacher must keep the tablet pointed at the page.

Evidence for learning gains is real but small. Most studies use one class, a pre-test and a post-test. A difference in normalised gain is a signal. To claim a learning gain you need random assignment, the same teacher for both groups, and marking done without knowing the group. Without those, a keen AR group can beat printed notes for reasons unrelated to AR.

sections.h3: Entertainment: track the street, the face, the field

blocks.text: Location-based games track GPS, the phone camera and inertial sensors. The game draws characters or clues on the street in front of you. The display is the phone. Evaluation is retention, play time and safety reports, because players walk while looking at a screen.

Camera filters track the face with a landmark model. The app draws a mask, glasses or a beard that follows the head. The display is the phone screen. The engineering target is frame rate and low jitter; a filter that slips by a few pixels looks broken. Live sports graphics track camera calibration and the field lines. The broadcaster draws a first-down line, a player name tag or a speed readout over the real field. The display is the television feed. Evaluation is alignment error and how often the graphic hides the play.

Stage and theme-park effects use projection mapping. A projector is calibrated to a physical set; the system draws light and characters onto walls, water or props. The tracked object is the set geometry. The audience sees the result without a device. Distraction and safety matter: a graphic that covers a stair or a moving actor is a hazard.

Assembly guidance tracks a marker on the bench or a plane found by SLAM. It draws the next bolt, the torque value, or the cable route over the real part. The display is a see-through headset or a tablet. Evaluation is error rate, assembly time and rework. Remote expert help shares the worker's camera view; the expert draws an arrow or circles a valve. The worker sees the mark on the same view. Evaluation is time to fix and the number of callbacks.

Warehouse picking shows the bin location and the count in a headset. The display is see-through, so the picker still sees the shelf. Inspection draws a checklist over the machine and marks the points to photograph. Training uses the same overlay on a real line, so the line does not stop for a dummy. Retail uses a phone to place a chair in a room; defence uses a helmet display for navigation and threat labels; navigation uses a phone camera to draw arrows on the road.

items: Costs: headsets, tablets, projectors, and spare batteries.
Content authoring: 3D models, step logic, and safety review take time.
Hygiene: shared headsets need cleaning between users.
Comfort: weight, heat and vergence strain limit long shifts.
Distraction: a label over a moving machine can hide a hazard.

examples.question: Sixty students are split into 30 using an AR anatomy app and 30 using printed notes. Both groups score a pre-test mean of 40 out of 100. The post-test mean is 78 for the AR group and 66 for the control group. Find the normalised gain for each group and compare the raw improvement.
steps: Pre-test mean is 40 out of 100. Maximum possible gain is 100 - 40 = 60 points.
AR normalised gain is 38 / 60 = 0.6333..., which rounds to 0.63.
Control normalised gain is 26 / 60 = 0.4333..., which rounds to 0.43.
Compare: 38 points against 26 points raw; 0.63 against 0.43 normalised.
examples.answer: The AR group has a normalised gain of 0.63 and the control group 0.43; the raw improvement is 38 points against 26 points, but with 30 students per group this is a signal, not proof.
examples.check:
pre = 40
post_ar = 78
post_control = 66
gain_ar = (post_ar - pre) / (100 - pre)
gain_control = (post_control - pre) / (100 - pre)
print(round(gain_ar, 2))
print(round(gain_control, 2))

traps: Answering with a list of app names. The marks are for what is tracked, what is drawn, which display type is used, and how the system was evaluated.
Treating normalised gain as the raw post-minus-pre difference. The denominator is 100 minus the pre-test score.
Assuming a marker can always be placed. In a sterile operating field a marker may be impossible, so surface tracking or SLAM may be needed.
Claiming a learning gain from a small pre/post study without random assignment, the same teacher and blinded marking.
Forgetting the display. A vein finder that projects onto the skin is projection AR, not a headset AR system.

quiz.q: State the three requirements that make a system AR.
quiz.a: Combine real and virtual; register the virtual object in 3D to the real world; run in real time.

quiz.q: Why does surgical AR need registration to the patient rather than only a good 3D model?
quiz.a: The overlay must sit on the actual tumour, vessel or cut plane. Without a patient-to-scan registration, the drawn model moves with the camera but not with the patient, so it is useless and unsafe.

quiz.q: A class has pre-test mean 50. The AR group post-test mean is 80 and the control group 70, out of 100. Find both normalised gains.
A study reports a large AR learning gain with 30 students per group. Give two reasons the result is only a signal.
quiz.a: The sample is small, so chance variation is large. The groups may differ in teacher, time on task or prior interest, and marking may not be blinded. Random assignment and blinded marking are needed before claiming a learning gain.

quiz.q: In an AR book, what is tracked and what is drawn?
quiz.a: The printed page image is tracked. The app draws a 3D model, label or animation fixed to that page.

quiz.q: For a live cricket or football graphic, name what is tracked, what is drawn and the display.
quiz.a: The camera and field geometry are tracked. The system draws a line, player tag or statistic over the field. The display is the broadcast television feed.

quiz.q: Why is a shared headset a hygiene problem in a hospital, and what is one practical response?
quiz.a: Many users touch the same headset near the face and eyes. A practical response is a cleanable face pad and a wipe-down procedure between users, or a personal tablet display where it fits the task.

quiz.q: Name two industry uses of AR.
quiz.a: Any two of: assembly guidance, remote expert help, warehouse picking, inspection, training without stopping the line.

beyond: Not for the exam. Regulatory approval for surgical AR is a long clinical-evidence process, not a graphics problem. Search for target registration error, mixed-reality surgical navigation and wireless display latency in classroom AR. The next engineering step is shared calibration: the same patient or machine model used by the headset, the tablet and the remote expert. Also look at authoring cost, because a good 3D step model often costs more than the headset.
